content:
As part of my PhD research under my advisor Frank Stephan I have formalised a number theory paper he co-authored, Improved Lower Bounds for Strong n-Conjectures. (arXiv version.)

https://github.com/Parcly-Taxel/Redhill

And while doing so I managed to optimise several constants and constructions. I have completed the entire project without using any AI whatsoever.

What is the recommended walkthrough in your repository if I want to understand what the project is about, without referring to the paper, reading the code only? There is a lot of definitions — I would like to know what to read first.

Martin Dvořák said:

What is the recommended walkthrough in your repository if I want to understand what the project is about, without referring to the paper, reading the code only? There is a lot of definitions — I would like to know what to read first.

Common.Quality contains the definitions of tuple and set-of-tuples quality.
Common.SubsumCondition defines the subsum and strong subsum conditions and proves various things about them.
Then the various sets used in the conjectures, as well as the conjectures themselves, are defined in Common.Conjectures.

Odd and General contain the meat of the paper – the disproofs of Ramaekers's conjecture for odd n≥5n\ge5n≥5 and n≥6n\ge6n≥6 respectively (n is the length of the tuple, n = 3 in the abc conjecture). Definitions (of the tuple seqeunce involved and auxiliary variables) are in *.Defs, the proof of the subsum condition is in *.Subsum, the ending steps of the proofs are in *.Main. There is an additional file specific to each folder.

In both cases the construction uses a chain of primes (Common.PrimeChain) where each prime is at least twice the last, as well as two special numbers v, w (Common.VWPair) derived from the chain. The original paper expressed the constructions with a few differences that I found were unnecessary, such as using a multiplier of 3 rather than 2 for the prime chain in the odd case, and proving an upper bound for w that neither proof uses.

There are two files not in any folder: KonyaginPrelude formalises an illustration of Konyagin's technique for n = 5 only (a "warm-up" proof, which was helpful in nailing down the definitions at the beginning), and BB94 formalises the main result from Browkin and Brzeziński's 1994 paper (which is cited in the present one).
Regarding VWPair, the paper used an imperative algorithm and somewhat tedious calculations to show the existence of v, w. I found that the Chinese remainder theorem suffices
